"You're going to the ward meeting again? It's Sunday, Rehana."
"It's about the old library building, Gopika. They want to turn it into a parking lot."
"And what will one meeting do?"
"Last time only six people came. If sixty come, the councillor has to listen." Rehana tied her dupatta and picked up a folder. "I've got photos of the carved doors, and the list of manuscripts Dada helped catalogue."
"You're not even an architect."
"No, but I teach the kids' reading hour there. Where will they go?"
Gopika sighed and reached for her own shoes. "Fine. I'm coming. But if it's boring, you're buying me chai."
"Deal. And bring your neighbour's son. He's fourteen. He should see how these decisions get made."
"You want to drag a teenager to a civic meeting?"
"I want him to know he's allowed to be in the room."

qa.q: What does the council want to turn the old library building into?
qa.a: They want to turn it into a parking lot.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel about bringing the fourteen-year-old to the meeting?
qa.a: She feels hopeful and determined, wanting him to know he is allowed to be in the room when civic decisions get made.

qa.q: What could Rehana do to bring more people like Gopika along next time?
qa.a: She could share the photos and the kids' reading hour story ahead of time, so people see exactly what is at stake before the meeting.

qa.q: How does Gopika's view of the meeting change during the scene?
qa.a: She starts doubtful that one meeting can do anything, but Rehana's reasons about the kids and the numbers win her over enough to put on her shoes.

grounding: It shows civic stewardship: joining local governance to preserve a heritage building and guiding the next generation.

passage: When I started the heritage walks, I thought it was just a hobby. I'd grown up in these lanes and knew every temple bell and every old haveli door. One Saturday I brought nine schoolkids, and one of them, Sahil, asked, "Kunal bhaiya, why are the carvings on this wall half broken?" I didn't know. That bothered me. So I spent two weeks in the city archive and at the municipal office, reading dull files and asking polite questions. It turned out a road widening had cut the building in half. I went back and told Sahil's group the whole story, then we wrote a short letter to the ward office asking for a plaque. It took four months, but the plaque went up. Sahil's now fourteen and he leads the first stretch of the walk himself. I just follow and fill in dates.

qa.q: How many schoolkids came on the Saturday walk when Sahil asked his question?
qa.a: Nine schoolkids came.

qa.q: Why did it bother Kunal that he couldn't answer Sahil's question?
qa.a: He felt responsible and uneasy about not knowing, since he cared about the lanes' history and the kids learning it properly.

qa.q: Which choice by Kunal worked best, and why?
qa.a: He researched the real answer and then involved the kids in writing to the ward office, which turned curiosity into a small, lasting civic result.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sahil to now lead part of the walk?
qa.a: He probably feels trusted and proud, knowing that a question he asked as a child became a plaque and a role he now holds. 😊

grounding: It illustrates preserving cultural legacy through the proper civic channels and passing it on to the next generation.

Project note, District Library Oral History Project. Written by Neelam, coordinator.
Amandeep, 24, joined us in March as a volunteer. Within weeks he had recorded eleven elders from the old weaving colony, including two who had never been interviewed before. What stood out was his patience: he sat through long pauses, asked permission before every recording, and returned each transcript to the family for corrections. In June he offered to train a group of college students. He did not lecture them; he paired each student with one elder and stayed in the corner, stepping in only when a student interrupted too much. He also filed our request with the municipal archive properly, forms and all, so the recordings will be kept on public record. Next step: I have asked him to write a short guide for new volunteers, and to lead the next training himself.

qa.q: How many elders had Amandeep recorded within weeks?
qa.a: He had recorded eleven elders from the old weaving colony.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's habit of returning transcripts to families suggest about what he cares about?
qa.a: It suggests he respects the elders' ownership of their stories and wants the record to be accurate, not just collected.

qa.q: How could Neelam support Amandeep as he takes on more leadership?
qa.a: Neelam could give him time to write the guide, check in after his first solo training, and keep backing his careful methods.

qa.q: How might one of the elders see this project?
qa.a: An elder who had never been interviewed might feel honoured that their memories are being kept and checked with their family.

grounding: It shows civic stewardship of cultural heritage and mentoring the next generation, through a coordinator's note.

14 November

Long day but a good one. Our heritage walk group finally got permission to clean the old stepwell behind the tehsil office. Twenty of us turned up at seven with gloves and sacks. Vaibhav brought his students from the government school, and I spent an hour showing them the carvings: the elephants, the woman carrying water pots. One boy asked, "Didi, who made this?" I said, "People from this town, three hundred years ago. And now it's your job to look after it." He looked at the stone like it belonged to him. That was my favourite moment.

In the afternoon I helped at the voter registration camp near the market. Only eleven people came, which was disappointing.

I'm tired, but I feel like I spent today on something that will last. Next month: the kids make a guidebook.

— Gargi

qa.a: Only eleven people came to the camp near the market.

qa.q: What does Gargi mean when she says she spent the day on something that will last?

qa.q: How could Gargi get more people to the next registration camp?
qa.a: She could ask the students or local shopkeepers to spread the word, or hold it alongside a heritage event people already enjoy.

qa.q: How might the boy who asked who made the stepwell see the town now?
qa.a: He seems to feel the heritage belongs to him, which may make him more likely to protect it as he grows up.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young woman preserving local heritage, supporting civic processes and guiding the next generation.

In the village of Bishnupur, the old terracotta temple had cracks running through its carved panels, and most children walked past without looking.
Bidisha, twenty-five, had come home after studying history in Kolkata. Every Sunday that winter she sat by the temple with a notebook, sketching each panel and asking the oldest potter, Haripada-jethu, what the scenes meant.
Then she asked Sonali, the primary schoolteacher, for help. They began bringing the Class 5 children on Saturdays. Each child adopted one panel, drew it and learned its story.
In February Bidisha wrote to the district heritage office with photos and the children's drawings, asking for the cracks to be repaired properly, not patched with cement.
A girl who used to throw stones at the pigeons there now stood in front of her panel and explained the story of Krishna and the cows to her father, her voice full of importance.

qa.q: What did each child adopt?
qa.a: Each child adopted one panel, drew it and learned its story.

qa.q: How did the girl who used to throw stones feel explaining her panel?
qa.a: She felt proud and important, sharing the story with her father.

qa.q: What made Bidisha's efforts likely to last?
qa.a: She involved the schoolteacher and children and wrote to the heritage office, so care for the temple did not rest on her alone.

qa.q: How might Haripada-jethu feel seeing children learn the panels' stories?
qa.a: He may feel honoured and hopeful that the stories he knows will be remembered.

grounding: A young woman preserves a village temple's heritage and guides the next generation to care for it.

Lindiwe noticed at her grandmother's funeral in Durban that nobody under forty knew the old wedding songs. The aunties sang them; the cousins stood silent, phones out.
She was twenty-six, a sound engineer. That winter she set up a recording corner in the community library every Saturday. She invited grandmothers to sing and tell where each song came from. Wei, a volunteer from the university, transcribed the words and translations.
Some weeks nobody came. Then Gogo Ntombi arrived with six friends and a thermos of tea, and sang for three hours.
By spring they had forty songs. Lindiwe didn't just store them online; she started a Sunday class where teenagers learned them from the grandmothers directly.
At her cousin's wedding in December, eight young people sang one of the songs while the aunties clapped and cried.

qa.q: How many songs did they have by spring?
qa.a: By spring they had forty songs.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when she noticed nobody under forty knew the songs?
qa.a: She felt saddened and worried that the songs would be lost with the older generation.

qa.q: Why was the Sunday class more important than just storing the recordings?
qa.a: It passed the songs directly from grandmothers to teenagers, keeping them alive in people, not only in files.

qa.q: How might the aunties have felt at the December wedding?
qa.a: They were moved to tears and joyful, hearing young people carry on the songs they had sung.

grounding: A young woman records and passes on her community's songs, preserving cultural legacy for the next generation.

On Monday mornings the district museum in Bhopal opened to rows of school buses, and Tanuja, twenty-four and the youngest education officer on staff, stood at the gate with a clipboard.
For months the tours had been a guard reading labels aloud. Children yawned by the second gallery. Kamal, the curator, had shrugged. “They don't care about old coins.”
Tanuja tried something else. She trained twelve older students from a nearby government school as junior guides, one gallery each. They learned the stories behind the tribal masks, the stone tools, the old maps. Each wore a small badge.
Kamal came to watch in the third week. A fourteen-year-old guide was explaining a bronze lamp to a class of eight-year-olds, who were leaning in to listen.
Kamal folded his arms. “All right,” he said to Tanuja. “Write me a proposal to make this permanent.”

qa.q: How many older students did Tanuja train as junior guides?
qa.a: She trained twelve older students.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when Kamal asked for a proposal?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and proud that her idea had won over a sceptical curator.

qa.q: What was clever about using older students as guides?
qa.a: It made the history lively for younger children and gave the guides a sense of ownership of their heritage.

qa.q: How does Kamal's view of the tours change?
qa.a: He moves from doubting that children care to asking for the programme to become permanent.

grounding: A young museum officer helps preserve heritage by training students to guide the next generation.

To: Mr Wasim Qureshi, Heritage Cell, Municipal Corporation, Ahmedabad
Dear Sir,
I am writing about the old stepwell behind the Kalupur market. It is over three hundred years old and is now full of plastic and rubble. Last month, I organised a walk there with twenty college students. Many of them had never heard of it. We would like to propose a restoration drive: our volunteers can clear rubbish on weekends if the Corporation provides safety equipment and an engineer's guidance. We would also like to create a small signboard telling its history, in Gujarati and English, and guide school groups monthly. I have attached photographs and a plan. I would be grateful for a meeting.
Yours sincerely,
Pradeep Shah

passage: "Gurleen, you asked on your show why I started the song circle. I'm Nilesh, twenty-five. My Dadi knew over two hundred folk songs from our village near Bhilwara. Wedding songs, harvest songs, lullabies. When she died, I realised nobody had written them down. Most were gone. That hit me hard. So I went back and recorded every elder who still remembered anything. Sixty songs so far. Then I thought: recordings aren't enough. Songs live when kids sing them. Now every Sunday, twenty children come to the community hall and I teach them two songs. Last week, a nine-year-old taught her grandmother a song the grandmother had forgotten. The old lady cried. I cried too. That's why."

qa.q: How many songs has Nilesh recorded so far?
qa.a: Sixty songs.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when realising Dadi's songs weren't written down?
qa.a: Nilesh felt deeply saddened and shaken by the loss.

qa.q: What makes Nilesh's approach effective for preserving heritage?
qa.a: Recording elders and also teaching children weekly, so the songs are sung and passed on, not just stored.

qa.q: How might the grandmother have felt when her granddaughter taught her the forgotten song?
qa.a: She was moved to tears, likely feeling joy at recovering part of her past.

grounding: A young man describes recording elders' folk songs and teaching them to children to preserve cultural heritage.

passage: I'm Himani, and I teach at the same Pune school where Shreya, twenty-five, volunteers on Saturdays. This year I watched her run a project she called "Know Your City." She took Class 8 on walks to the old wada, the municipal office and a polling booth. She got a retired judge to explain how the constitution came to be, and asked the students to interview their grandparents about Partition and the old city. Then they made a small exhibition. On the last day, one shy boy stood up and said, "Now I want to vote when I turn eighteen." Shreya just nodded, but I saw her smile when she turned away. I don't know what she felt inside, but she stayed back cleaning up long after everyone left.

qa.q: What might Shreya have felt when the shy boy spoke?

First week: Joseph, a young architect, was hired by the municipality to survey an old Portuguese-era market building slated for demolition. Most officials wanted a mall. Joseph wasn't sure what he thought.
Two weeks later: He met Sachin, an eighty-year-old shopkeeper who had sold spices there for sixty years. Sachin showed him carved beams and old ledgers. Joseph photographed everything and couldn't stop thinking about it.
A month later: Joseph presented a plan to the council: restore the market, keep the old traders, add a small heritage museum run by local students. Some councillors laughed. The commissioner asked for a cost estimate. Joseph left the meeting with his hands trembling and a second meeting booked.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling after meeting Sachin?

qa.q: What made Joseph's plan thoughtful?

Siddharth, beta, you asked why I care so much about the village temple dance. Let me tell you.
When I was a young woman of twenty-five, I, Sharmila, was a software engineer in Bengaluru. The old dance teacher in our village wrote to me: no one was learning anymore. The festival dance would die with her.
I nearly ignored it. I was busy. Then I came home for the festival and saw only three old women dancing.
So I made a choice. I spent every long weekend for three years in the village, learning from her, recording every step, and teaching the girls at the government school.
Now forty children dance at the festival.
So when you complain about coming home for Onam, remember: someone has to carry it.

qa.q: How many children dance at the festival now?
qa.a: Forty children.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel seeing only three old women dancing?
qa.a: She likely felt sad and alarmed that the tradition was dying.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Sharmila's story?
qa.a: Choosing to spend long weekends for three years learning from the teacher and teaching schoolgirls.

qa.q: How might the old dance teacher have felt about Sharmila coming back?
qa.a: The teacher likely felt relieved and grateful that the dance would live on.

The heritage walk Shreya had organised was set for Sunday morning. On Saturday night, heavy rain flooded half the old city lanes, and her co-organiser, Farhan, called in sick.
Shreya had promised twenty college students a tour of the stepwells and havelis, along with a talk by an elderly historian.
At six a.m. she walked the route herself in gumboots, marking which lanes were passable. She rerouted the walk to the covered bazaar and moved the historian's talk to a haveli courtyard.
Nineteen students came, damp and cheerful. The historian told them stories about the families who built the wells.
Afterward, three students asked Shreya if they could help run the next walk. She felt tired to her bones, and certain it had been worth it.

The monsoon had just ended when Chandrika led her Saturday walk into the old city lane behind Charminar Road, twenty schoolchildren in a wobbly line behind her. She stopped at a stepwell choked with plastic bags and broken tiles.
"My grandfather drew water here," she told them. "Now look."
For a year she had pushed the ward office for permission to clean it. Akash, a volunteer from the municipal heritage cell, finally got it signed. Today the children would scrub the first three steps and record the carvings in their notebooks.
A boy asked, "Why should we care? It's just old stones."
Chandrika crouched beside him. "Because someone cared for it before you. Now it's your turn to keep it for the next children."
By noon, a carved fish had appeared under the dirt. The children crowded round, shouting. Akash took photos for the ward's heritage register, and Chandrika wrote each child's name beside them.

qa.q: What appeared under the dirt by noon?
qa.a: A carved fish appeared under the dirt.

qa.q: What was the boy likely feeling when he asked why he should care?
qa.a: He was probably bored and doubtful, not yet seeing why old stones mattered to him.

qa.q: How could Chandrika keep the children involved after this walk?
qa.a: She could bring the same group back for the next steps and let them present their notebook records to the ward, so they feel like the well's keepers.

qa.q: What is it like for the children when the carved fish appears?
qa.a: The children feel excited and proud, crowding round and shouting, because their own scrubbing uncovered something hidden. 🎉

grounding: Shows a young adult preserving local heritage with the civic office and handing that care on to the next generation.
